title: Nehemiah 9:9–15
context: The prayer recalls the exodus: God saw the affliction of the fathers in Egypt, heard their cry by the Red Sea, showed signs against Pharaoh, divided the sea, led them by the pillar of cloud and fire, came down on Mount Sinai to give right ordinances and true laws, made known the Sabbath, gave bread from the sky and water from the rock, and commanded them to possess the land he had sworn to give. Each line draws on the accounts in Exodus and Numbers (compare Exodus 3:7; 13:21; 15:5; 19:20; 17:6). The emphasis falls on God’s initiative, goodness, and generosity before Israel’s failures are named. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about God’s saving acts, his good law, and his faithful provision. Both traditions commonly see the manna and the water from the rock pointing forward to Christ (compare John 6:32; 1 Corinthians 10:4), while honoring their first meaning in Israel’s history.

verses.text: “You saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heard their cry by the Red Sea,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God seeing the affliction of the fathers in Egypt and hearing their cry by the Red Sea. God responds to his people’s distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s attentive care as rooted in his covenant faithfulness (compare Exodus 3:7). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as comfort for the suffering.

verses.text: and showed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against all his servants, and against all the people of his land, for you knew that they dealt proudly against them, and made a name for yourself, as it is today.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God showing signs against Pharaoh because the Egyptians dealt proudly. God opposes the proud oppression of his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God making a name for himself through the exodus. Both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating God’s justice and glory.

verses.text: You divided the sea before them, so that they went through the middle of the sea on the dry land; and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into the mighty waters.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God dividing the sea and casting the pursuers into the depths like a stone. Deliverance is complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language as echoing the song of Moses (compare Exodus 15:5). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as praise for God’s mighty salvation.

verses.text: Moreover, in a pillar of cloud you led them by day; and in a pillar of fire by night, to give them light in the way in which they should go.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God leading the people by the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Guidance is constant through every stage of the journey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pillar as God’s visible presence with his people (compare Exodus 13:21). Both traditions commonly read the verse as assurance of God’s faithful guidance.

verses.text: “You also came down on Mount Sinai, and spoke with them from heaven, and gave them right ordinances and true laws, good statutes and commandments,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God coming down on Sinai and giving right ordinances and true laws. The law is a good gift from a gracious God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the giving of the law as an act of grace to a redeemed people (compare Exodus 19:20). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as honoring the goodness of God’s law.

verses.text: and made known to them your holy Sabbath, and commanded them commandments, statutes, and a law, by Moses your servant,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God making known his holy Sabbath and commanding statutes by Moses. God shares his rest with his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Sabbath as a gift that marks Israel as God’s people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating God’s revelation through Moses.

verses.text: and gave them bread from the sky for their hunger, and brought water out of the rock for them for their thirst, and commanded them that they should go in to possess the land which you had sworn to give them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God giving bread from the sky and water from the rock and commanding the people to possess the land. Provision and promise go together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the manna and water as pointing forward to Christ (compare John 6:32; 1 Corinthians 10:4). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as praise for God’s generous care.
